# Wiki Authoring Specification

The rules that decide whether a page you write is conformant. This lookup holds the readability rules every page meets and the boundary-statement rule, and names every other author-facing lookup below, each for the concern it covers. Every page template points at these files by anchor; how the engine reads a page's frontmatter is `wiki-page-spec`.

These files are materialized into the wiki itself at `<wiki.location>/_authoring/`, framework-owned and refreshed by the wiki's scaffold step, so they are readable without an agent.

**See also:** `wiki-conventions` — for how links between pages are formed and resolved.
**See also:** `wiki-page-placement` — for where a page may sit and what it may depend on.
**See also:** `wiki-scaffold-files` — for the files every sub-wiki contains.
**See also:** `wiki-page-content-rules` — for callouts, code citations and product-page wording.
**See also:** `wiki-page-ids` — for row and criterion ids, and how they move when a page is split or merged.
**See also:** `wiki-fact-placement` — for where a fact sits: one home per surface, fold pointers, realization membership.
**See also:** `wiki-page-state` — for what is not true yet when a page is written: the page state axes and decisions registers.
**See also:** `wiki-section-disposition` — for which sections a page may drop, and the placeholders it must replace.
**See also:** `wiki-template-labels` — for the grammar of a template's docblock labels.
**See also:** `wiki-cell-grammars` — for how a template fixes a cell's form.
**See also:** `wiki-surface-cell-grammars` — for the cell grammars of a design surface's actions and flow steps.
**See also:** `wiki-surface-placement-cell-grammars` — for the bullets that place a design surface.
**See also:** `wiki-sitemap-cell-grammars` — for the cell grammars of a sitemap table and the node a surface cites.
**See also:** `wiki-journey-cell-grammars` — for the cell grammars of a journey's stages and the stages a surface cites.
**See also:** `wiki-layout-pattern-cell-grammars` — for the cell grammars of a layout pattern's regions and the regions its navigation sits in.
**See also:** `wiki-entity-cell-grammars` — for the cell grammars that name entities and their fields.
**See also:** `wiki-page-types` — for each page type's purpose, default authorship and freshness.
**See also:** `wiki-entity-data-model` — for what an entity page's field table means.
**See also:** `wiki-write-protocol` — for which skill may write what.
**See also:** `wiki-authorship-routing` — for which page type a piece of content routes to.
**See also:** `wiki-fact-ownership` — for where a fact two page types both ask for lives.

## Boundary statements

A page's `## Boundaries` states what the page's subject deliberately does not cover and which page
owns that instead — linked, not described. It reads at whatever scope the page owns, and the
templates that declare the section are where to look for which types carry it. One bullet names one
excluded thing and its owner; a paragraph describing what the neighbor does belongs on the
neighbor, which is the page the bullet links.

The section is not a second home for content another convention already places. Where a sub-wiki's
README routes a class of content — a policy rule, an entity invariant, a criterion, a role gate —
that routing governs, and a boundary bullet restating one of them puts a fact in two places. No
check decides this: whether a bullet restates a criterion already on the page is a judgment, so
review is the compensating control.

Two neighboring sections are distinct from it. `## Non-examples`, on a type declaring both, names
near-misses a reader might mistake FOR the subject; boundaries name scope the subject genuinely
excludes and who holds it — a page can need both, and on a type that declares both the sections sit
adjacent. A section recording what a downstream author is delegated to decide is a third thing
again: name it for the delegation rather than sharing this word, so a reader moving between two
page types does not meet one header meaning two things.

## Authoring for readability

Keeps pages and indexes scannable. `/wiki-lint` Pass 1 enforces the deterministic rules (`related-order`, `related-annotation`, `body-h1`, `frontmatter-restatement` at error severity; `lead-line` as a warning); the presentation defaults are documented-only, with page size surfaced informationally by `/wiki-review`.

### Filenames and links

- Filenames: `kebab-case.md`, the slug derived from the title when the page is created. It stays stable — a later title edit does not rename the file — because the slug path is the page's identity, cited by `@verifies` and `Verifies` references. Directories (`kebab-case/`) group pages by type, so the filename takes **no redundant type prefix** (`entities/cart.md`, not `entities/entity-cart.md`). Pages with a shared title-token cluster sort together naturally; group by _titling_, never by a prefix.
- **Never hard-delete** — replace with a `redirect` stub.

### Related ordering

`related:` frontmatter lists and `## Related …` body sections share one canonical order: intra-wiki entries first (no domain prefix, alphabetical by path), then cross-wiki entries grouped by sub-wiki prefix (groups alphabetical), alphabetical by path within each group. Applies to every page type — the `related:` block and `## Related …` sections are wiki-owned even on `mirror-source` pages.

### Annotated Related bullets

Every bullet under a `## Related …` header is `[[link]] — <why it's related>`. Multi-link bullets share one annotation: `[[a]] / [[b]] — both containers`. Annotations are body-only — `related:` frontmatter entries carry no annotation.

### Lead sentence

The first prose line's opening sentence is self-contained and at most 120 characters as the index shows it: a wiki link is shown as the title of the page it names (the last path segment, hyphens as spaces, when that page does not exist), so a long title counts toward the limit; `*`/`_` emphasis markers are stripped outside inline code, and an inline code span is kept whole and counted, backticks included. The index excerpts exactly this sentence — reindexing takes the first sentence of the first prose line and, past the limit, cuts it at the last space under the limit outside a code span, never splitting a span — so the lead sentence _is_ the page's index entry. Front-load the page's definition; qualifications go in the second sentence.

A type whose first body section is a pointer rather than prose (`source-summary` opens with `## Source`, a bare URL) declares a `summarySection` instead: the lint measures the lead sentence from that section's first prose line, not the top of the body. `source-summary`'s summary section is `## Key takeaways`; `mirror-source`'s is `## Summary`. The same rule applies there — front-load a self-contained opening sentence, qualifications after.

### Heading and metadata hygiene

The body starts at H2 — the title lives in frontmatter, so a body H1 duplicates it. No frontmatter facts restated in the body: `**Date:**` / `**Created:**` / `**Updated:**` / `**Owner:**` lines duplicate structured fields and drift. Template section fields like `**Source:**` or `**Last verified:**` are designed body content, not restatements.

### Presentation defaults

Documented-only — judgment-bearing, never linted:

- **Enumerable or comparative facts → table.** Items with shared attributes read faster as rows than as prose.
- **Flows, hierarchies, state → fenced `mermaid` diagram**, capped at ~15 nodes; decompose beyond that. Never use mermaid's `[[ ]]` node shape — it collides with wiki-link syntax.
- **No empty structure.** An empty table or placeholder diagram is structure-shaped noise; add it when the content exists.
- **Split pages that outgrow one subject.** Length alone is not a defect (research syntheses run long legitimately); a page covering more than one subject is. `/wiki-review` lists the largest pages informationally.
  See `wiki-page-ids` §Splitting and merging for how to carry the ids across.

### Exemptions

`mirror-source` pages track external sources verbatim — exempt from the body-style checks (`body-h1`, `frontmatter-restatement`, `lead-line`). `redirect` stubs are exempt from `lead-line` (boilerplate body). Related ordering and annotation apply to all page types.
